First Chapter.
Knowledge is one, eternal, devoid of beginning and end; there exists no other reality whatsoever that is true.
This differentiation of cognition within this [consciousness] appears indeed through the limiting adjunct of the sense organs, and not otherwise.
Then I, devoted to my disciples, shall speak the instruction on yoga;
[I am] the Lord of all beings, the bestower of liberation upon the self. (1-2)

Having abandoned the doctrine of those whose nature is contentious and which is rooted in the difficult-to-understand [self], for the sake of self-knowledge of all beings whose minds have no other resort— 1.3.
Some praise truth, while others praise austerity and purity; some praise forgiveness, and likewise equanimity and straightforwardness.
Some praise generosity, while others likewise praise rites for the ancestors;
some praise ritual action, and others supreme detachment.
Some wise ones praise the duties of a householder;
likewise, some consider rituals such as the Agnihotra to be supreme. (1.6)
They praise mantra-yoga and the practice of visiting certain sacred fords;
indeed, they proclaim many such means for the sake of liberation. (1.7)
Thus resolved in this world, people who discern what ought and ought not to be done, though freed from evil deeds, nevertheless fall into delusion. (1.8)
He who adheres to this view, having obtained both sin and merit, wanders here helplessly through the succession of birth and death. (1.9)
By other eminent thinkers intent on the protection of their own views, many selves have been declared to be eternal and likewise all-pervading. (1.10)
Whatever is an object of direct perception, they declare that nothing else exists; for what reason, then, do others with certain minds maintain that heaven and such things exist? (1.11)
Others [hold that] the flow of consciousness is [the ultimate]; some know the supreme to be the Void;
others consider the two—Prakṛti and Puruṣa—to be the reality. (1.12)
Those whose minds are utterly divided and who are averse to the ultimate truth,
as well as others, having reflected thus according to their own intelligence and according to what they have heard— (1.13)
Some declare this world to be without a Lord (nirīśvara), while others likewise say it has a Lord (seśvara);
fearing the instability [of their own positions], they speak with various distinctions based on sound reasoning. (1.14)
These and other sages are described in the scriptures under various distinct names; indeed, these are intended to cause confusion among the world.
It is impossible to state the opinion of those whose nature is such dispute;
all people wandering in this [world] are excluded from the path to liberation. (1-16)
Having examined all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this one alone has been perfectly established as the supreme Yoga scripture. (1.17)
When that [Self] has departed, all this certainly departs;
effort should be directed toward that—what else has been spoken in the scriptures? (1.18)
This Yoga scripture, expounded by us, is to be kept secret;
it should be given only to one who is a true devotee and a great soul within the three worlds.
The Veda is considered to be twofold: the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) and the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa).
There are two further divisions within the section on knowledge and the section on ritual action. (1.20)
The section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is of two kinds, consisting of prohibitions and injunctions. || 1-21 ||
In the performance of forbidden actions, sin certainly arises;
in the performance of actions according to the prescribed rule, merit certainly arises. (1-22)
The ritual aggregate (vidhikūṭa) is threefold, consisting of the obligatory, the occasional, and the optional.
If the obligatory rite is not performed, there is sin; whereas for the optional and occasional rites, there is a specific fruit.
The fruit [of action] should be known to be twofold: heaven and indeed hell;
heaven is of many kinds, and hell likewise may be so. (1.24)
Heaven is indeed for meritorious deeds, and hell for sinful deeds;
this creation consists of the bondage of karma and certainly does not exist otherwise.
And living beings experience various pleasures in heaven,
as well as indeed various kinds of unbearable sufferings in hell.
Suffering arises from the power of evil karma, and happiness arises from the power of meritorious karma;
therefore, one who desires happiness should certainly perform various kinds of merit. (1.27)
But at the conclusion of the experience of evil, there will indeed be rebirth;
however, at the conclusion of the experience of merit, it certainly does not happen otherwise. (1.28)
Even in heaven, there is the experience of suffering in such things as witnessing the superior splendor of others;
therefore, all this is suffering—of this there is no doubt. (1.29)
That which is described by those who prescribe ritual actions is twofold: merit and demerit.
Through these merits and demerits, bondage arises for embodied beings in due course.
One who is averse to the fruits of actions in this world or the next should renounce all fruitful karma;
having abandoned even that which is designated as obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika), one should proceed toward yoga.
Having understood the greatness of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), the wise yogi should renounce it;
having abandoned both merit and demerit, he proceeds to the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa). || 1.32 ||
"The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen, heard," and so forth—this Śruti should be practiced with great effort; it bestows liberation and provides the cause [for its attainment]. (1.33)
He who impels the functioning of the intellect toward both sinful and meritorious acts—that I am; from me proceeds the entire world, including all things moving and stationary.
Everything is seen from me, and everything dissolves into me;
I am not distinct from this, nor is there anything whatsoever distinct from me. (1.34)
Just as in countless water-filled bowls there might appear the multiplicity of a single [reflection], so too no such distinction is seen here in the Veda.
Just as that supreme number which exists in the limiting adjuncts, such as clay bowls, becomes [manifested] in the sun, so too is it in the Self. (1.35)
Just as a single dreamer is perceived in various ways within a dream, so too, even in the waking state, the one [Self] appears as the manifold world. (1.36)
Just as the notion of a snake arises in a rope, or the delusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, so too is this entire universe manifested within the Supreme Self. (1.37)
Just as the illusory form of a snake ceases upon the knowledge that it is a rope, so too does this false world vanish through the knowledge of the Self. (1.38)
Just as this delusion of silver vanishes through the knowledge of the mother-of-pearl shell, so too does this delusion of the world always vanish through the knowledge of the Self. 1-39
Just as the illusion of a bamboo pole may arise from the application of frog-fat collyrium, so too is this world an illusion arising from the collyrium of habitual conceptualization. (1.40)
Just as the serpent ceases to exist through the knowledge of the rope,
and just as white appears yellow due to a defect of the eye and not otherwise,
so too, through the defect of ignorance, the Self becomes the world which is difficult to abandon. (1.41)

Just as a patient perceives whiteness for himself upon the destruction of his disorder, so too is the Self realized through the destruction of ignorance by means of the knowledge of that whiteness. (1.42)
Just as a rope can never become a snake at any of the three times, so too the Self—which transcends the qualities (guṇas) and is stainless—can never become the universe. (1.43)
That Īśvara and the others are impermanent because they undergo coming and going, and that this is determined by some realization of the Self through the scripture—this has been ascertained. (1.44)
Just as foam and bubbles arise in the ocean by the power of the wind, so too does this world-process, fragile as a moment, arise within the Self. (1.45)
Non-difference alone shines forth eternally; the difference between objects does not shine forth.
This differentiation into two, three, and so on, results ultimately in error. (1.46)
Whatever has been and whatever is yet to be, as well as the formed and the formless—
all this entire world is indeed manifested within the Supreme Self.
The knowledge fashioned by the Kalpakas has become false and illusory in nature;
how can this world, which has that as its root, be real? (1.48)
This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, has arisen from consciousness;
therefore, having abandoned everything else, one should take refuge in that consciousness. (1.49)
Just as space functions both inside and outside a jar, so too does the Self eternally function both inside and outside the entire range of effects. (1.50)
Just as space is unattached within the five elements which are illusory, so too the Self is unattached within the aggregate of effects; it is not otherwise.
The entire universe, beginning with Ishvara, is pervaded on all sides by the Self;
there exists the One, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, complete and devoid of duality.
Since there is no other illuminator, it must therefore be self-luminous;
because it is self-luminous, the Self has the nature of light. (1.53)
Since there is no interruption whatsoever for the Self in terms of its nature throughout the ten periods of time, the Self must indeed be complete in every respect. (1-54)
Since destruction does not exist through the five elements, which are by nature void, therefore the self must be eternal; indeed, its destruction cannot occur. (1.55)
Since there is nothing else here besides that, therefore it alone exists at all times;
since anything other than that would be false, the Self must indeed be real. (1.56)

Since happiness arises from the destruction of suffering within this unreal saṃsāra born of ignorance, and since through knowledge that [suffering] becomes void from beginning to end, therefore the Self must be happiness. (1.57)
Since ignorance, the cause of the universe, has been destroyed by knowledge, therefore the Self becomes knowledge; and because of that, knowledge is eternal. (1.58)
When this universe appears as manifold in terms of time, there exists that one Self alone, which is beyond the path of conceptual construction. (1.59)
All external beings go to destruction in the course of time;
for the Self, which is devoid of duality, is that from which words turn back. 1.60
It is neither space, nor wind, nor fire, nor water, nor earth;
it is neither this effect, nor the Lord (Īśvara), and so forth; indeed, it is the one, perfect Self. (1.61)
The yogi, having renounced all mental constructs and abandoned the false grasp of worldly existence, perceives the Self within himself with certainty. (1.62)

Having perceived the Self within both the self and the non-self as consisting of infinite bliss, he forgets the universe and rejoices through the intensity of his meditative absorption (samādhi). || 1.63 ||
Illusion alone is the mother of the universe; there is no other reality according to the wisdom of truth.
When the universe undergoes destruction, then indeed it does not exist. (1.64)
Since all this is to be abandoned, as it is merely the play of Māyā, therefore that which consists of the body, wealth, and pleasure is not an object of true affection. (1.65)
This world consists of three types— enemy, friend, and neutral—
and this is invariably observed in worldly dealings, and not otherwise.
However, the distinction between the pleasant, the unpleasant, and so forth, is clearly fixed among objects. (1.66)
In this way, sons and other such things come into being solely through the influence of the adjuncts of the self, and not otherwise.
Having thus understood the universe as the play of Māyā by means of both scripture and reasoning, [one attains liberation].
By means of superimposition and negation, yogis bring about dissolution.
When the Puruṣa is indeed entirely devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), then he, being stainless and consisting of indivisible knowledge, desires to speak. (1.68)
Thus, the Puruṣa himself, desiring, creates offspring;
since ignorance appears [therein], it is therefore false by its very nature. (1.69)
Connected with the state of pure Brahman and endowed with knowledge, one becomes that very Brahman; by means of that, one goes to the Truth from which the sky appears.
Therefore, air shines forth; from air, fire; from that, water; from that, earth shines forth. This conceptualization exists when [the ground] is established. (1.71)
From space arises wind; from the wind of space, fire is produced;
from space, wind, and fire comes water; and from space, wind, fire, and water, the earth is formed.
Space has sound as its characteristic; wind is flickering and has touch as its characteristic;
fire has form as its characteristic; and water has taste as its characteristic.
Earth, characterized by its quality of fragrance, certainly does not become otherwise.
Space is said to have one quality; wind is said to have two qualities;
likewise, fire has three qualities, and the waters possess four qualities.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell—this earth, possessing these five qualities, is now fashioned by the creators. (1.74)
Form is perceived by the eye, odor is perceived by the nose, taste by the tongue, and touch is supremely grasped by the skin. (1.75)
Sound is grasped by the ear; it necessarily appears [in that way] and not otherwise.
This entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, has arisen from consciousness.
If it exists, this would be a mere mental construction; if it does not exist, then that which consists of consciousness truly exists.
The earth was shattered; water merged into fire;
fire likewise dissolved into air; and air went to its dissolution in space.
In ignorance, the great ether dissolves into the supreme state.

The power of Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) consists of the veil of distraction; she is of the nature of insufferable suffering, insentient in form, and composed of the qualities of passion, purity, and darkness. (1.79)

Veiled by the power of the covering of illusion (māyāvaraṇa-śakti), that [consciousness], whose nature is non-cognition, manifests in the form of the world through its inherent quality of projection (vikṣepa). || 1.80 ||
That knowledge in which the quality of tamas predominates is Durgā herself;
the Lord is certainly that consciousness conditioned by her.
That knowledge which is superior to existence is Lakṣmī, who possesses a divine form;
consciousness when endowed with that [knowledge] becomes Viṣṇu, and not otherwise. (1.81)
That knowledge which abounds in the quality of rajas should be known as Sarasvatī;
he who is of the nature of consciousness is Brahman, the sustainer of that [knowledge]. (1.82)
All the gods, beginning with Īśa, are seen within the Supreme Self;
all that is insentient, such as the body and so forth, is that very Vidyā manifesting in various ways. (1.83)
In this manner, the creators imagine the origin of the universe;
thus, reality and unreality arise here through imaginings impelled by another. (1.84)
Every object is manifested in the form of "knowability" and so forth;
a distinction arises only when specific words are employed, and not otherwise. (1.85)
In the same way, there is no other illuminator or producer of an object;
rather, the object is manifested as its own nature by means of its own form. (1.86)
There exists but one, whose nature is bliss filled with pure being, perfect and all-pervading; there is nothing else.
He who constantly maintains this knowledge shall be liberated from the suffering of death and worldly existence. (1.87)
That one alone exists, and nothing else; it is realized by the mind as that wherein all things have gone to dissolution through superimposition and denial. (1.88)
From the father’s sheath composed of food, born of past karma, that body arises—beautiful for the sake of experiencing its own prior [karmic] fruits, yet filled with manifold suffering. (1.89)
This mansion of enjoyment, constructed from flesh, bone, sinew, marrow, and the like, is strung together with a continuous network of channels solely for the experience of suffering. (1.90)
This body, belonging to the supreme state, is composed of the five elements;
known as the "Cosmic Egg" (brahmāṇḍa), it is fashioned for the experience of suffering and pleasure.
Bindu is Śiva and rajas is Śakti; from the union of these two, the dream-like worlds arise spontaneously through its own insentient power. (1.92)
Through that quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), the gross objects situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) are, in brief, innumerable; therein resides the individual soul (jīva) along with its karmas.
From those five elements, everything exists for the enjoyment of that which is designated as the individual soul (jīva).
In accordance with past karma, I bring about these events;
though abiding in all beings, I am not insentient, yet I experience them through the state of being insentient.
Bound by its own actions, that which is called the individual soul (jīva) becomes manifold from the insentient matter;
for the sake of experience, it undergoes action again and again within what is known as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
And the individual soul dissolves at the conclusion of its experience of the fruits of its own karma.
The second chapter:
Within this body exists Mount Meru, together with the seven continents; the rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fields, and the guardians of those fields. (2.1)
All the sages, the ascetics, the constellations, and likewise the planets; the holy pilgrimage sites, the sacred seats (pīṭhas), and the deities of those seats abide here. (2–2)
The moon and the sun, wandering as the agents of creation and destruction, as well as space, wind, fire, water, and earth; 2-3.
Whatever beings exist in the three worlds, they all proceed from the body;
encompassing Mount Meru, worldly activity proceeds everywhere.
He who knows all this is a yogi; there is no doubt about this. || 2-5 ||

In the body known as the Cosmic Egg (brahmāṇḍa), situated according to its respective location on the peak of Mount Meru, the Moon, possessing eight external digits, stands with its nectar-rayed form.
He too revolves day and night, raining nectar while facing downwards;
from that, the nectar becomes twofold and indeed proceeds in a subtle manner.
For the sake of nourishment, the water of the Mandākinī flows through the path of the iḍā;
it certainly nourishes the entire body by means of the iḍā path. (2-8)
For this moon, the possessor of nectar, is situated on the left side.
Another [moon], appearing like pure milk, forcibly draws [the nectar] from the mandala;
for the sake of creation, the moon proceeds to Mount Meru by way of the central path. (2.9)
Situated at the base of Mount Meru and endowed with twelve digits (kalās), the Sun,
the Lord of Creatures, moves upward along the southern path by means of his rays.
The sun certainly swallows the exudations of the moon and the minerals;
it revolves within the solar orb and within every physical form.
This supreme form of the Sun carries Nirvāṇa on the southern path;
through its conjunction with the ascendant, it effects both creation and dissolution. (2.12)
Within the bodies of human beings, there are three hundred and fifty channels (nāḍīs);
among them, fourteen are the principal channels. (2.13)
Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Gāndhārī, Hastijihvikā, Kuhū, Sarasvatī, Pūṣā, Śaṅkhinī, and Payasvinī. (2.14)
Vāruṇī, Lambusā, Viśvodarī, and Yaśasvinī—among these, Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Suṣumṇikā are the three principal ones. (2.15)
Among the three, Suṣumṇā alone is the primary one; she is beloved by the yogis.
The other channels of embodied beings exist indeed by depending upon her. (2-16)
Those channels, resembling lotus fibers, are situated with their openings facing downward;
they rest upon the spinal column and take the form of the moon, the sun, and fire. (2.17)
Among them, the channel that has gone to the center is Citrā; she is my beloved.
And right there is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), auspicious and subtler than the subtlest.
Brilliant with five colors, pure, moving through the center, that Suṣumṇā is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the body; that Suṣumṇā has the form of the center. (2-19)
This is declared to be the divine path that brings about the bliss of immortality;
by mere meditation, the lord of yogis shall destroy the flood of his sins. (2-20)
Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis,
there exists the foundation (ādhāra), four finger-breadths in width and level.
And upon the pericarp of that foundational lotus, there exists a most beautiful triangular *yoni*, hidden in all the tantras. (2.22)
There, the supreme deity Kuṇḍalinī has the form of a flash of lightning;
she is three and a half cubits long, coiled, and situated upon the path of the Suṣumṇā. (2.23)
She, whose form is the manifestation of the world, is ever intent upon creation;
she is the Goddess of Speech, who cannot be expressed by words, and is eternally saluted by the gods. (2.24)
The channel named Iḍā, situated on the left path, embraces the Suṣumṇā and extends to the right nostril. (2.25)
The channel named Piṅgalā, which is situated on the right path, embraces the central channel and extends to the left nostril. (2.26)
Indeed, that which is the Suṣumṇā situated between the Iḍā and Piṅgalā, yogis know as the six powers and the six lotuses within the six locations. (2.27)
The Suṣumṇā has five locations and many names;
these should be understood from the scriptures according to their specific requirements. (2.28)
There is another channel, distinct from that, which arises from the *mūlādhāra*;
it reaches the tongue, the genitals, the eyes, the big toes, and the ears.
Having obtained [the body] with its belly, armpits, thumbs, ears, all limbs, anus, and stomach, they indeed return according to the place of their origin. (2.29)

From these very channels, proceeding from the primary and secondary branches in succession, three hundred and fifty thousand [channels] have arisen, established according to their respective portions. (2–30)
These channels, which carry the vital fluids and are adept at the movement of the winds, remain within this body, interwoven like warp and woof and thoroughly pervading it. (2.31)
Situated in the center of the solar orb and endowed with twelve digits (kalās),
the blazing fire that digests food resides in the region of the bladder.
This Vaiśvānara fire is indeed born from a portion of my own splendor;
residing within the bodies of living beings, it performs various kinds of digestion.
The fire that bestows longevity grants strength and nourishment, as well as physical agility, having destroyed the arising of diseases. (2-33)
Therefore, having duly kindled the Vaiśvānara fire, the wise yogi should daily offer food into it according to the instructions of his guru. (2.34)
Within this body known as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there are many locations;
those which I have declared as the primary ones should be understood here in this scripture. (2-35)
There exist various names and diverse locations within the cosmic manifestation; it is simply impossible to describe them all. (2.36)
When the body has been thus fashioned, the all-pervading *jīva* dwells within it, adorned by the garland of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and bound by the shackles of karma. (2.37)
Endowed with various kinds of qualities, he is the performer of all activities;
he experiences the diverse karmas acquired in previous lives. (2.38)
Whatever is perceived in the world, all that arises from karma;
indeed, every living being experiences enjoyments in accordance with their karma. (2.39)
Whatever defects, such as desire and the like, bestow pleasure and pain, all of them proceed in accordance with the karma of the living being. (2.40)
When consciousness is suffused with merit, it nourishes the vital breaths alone;
having obtained an external object of enjoyment consisting of merit, it becomes self-sustaining. (2.41)
Therefore, by the power of karma, pleasure or even pain arises for a person;
consciousness, being stained by sin, certainly does not remain [unaffected].
Nor would that [effect] be different from it, nor is there anything whatsoever different from it;
every object is produced from consciousness conditioned by māyā. (2-42)
Just as various things arise for the enjoyment of living beings at their proper time,
so too does the superimposition of silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell occur through the power of defects.
Likewise, due to the defects of one's own karma, the world is indeed superimposed upon Brahman.

If such knowledge as this, which is fully capable of uprooting even that which has arisen along with its latent impressions (vāsanā), were to arise, it would be the means for achieving liberation. (2.44)
The direct perception of a specific [object] is the cause for a direct experience that is an error; it is not otherwise. This truth has been spoken by me, truly, truly. (2.45)
In the case of a perceptual error, one should destroy it by means of direct perception;
for as long as that [error] exists, the delusion of saṃsāra will never cease. (2-46)
The cessation of false knowledge, however, occurs through the perception of the specific reality; otherwise, there would be no cessation, for the delusion of silver is observed [to persist]. (2.47)
As long as knowledge regarding the stainless direct realization has not arisen, all various beings continue to be perceived. (2.48)
When the body acquired through karma becomes a means for attaining nirvāṇa, then the bearing of this body is fruitful; it is not otherwise. (2-49)

Whatever kind of latent impression (vāsanā) exists as the root attached to the individual soul (jīva), according to that very [impression], the living being experiences delusion regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. (2.50)
If a practitioner of yoga desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, he should perform the duties of his caste and stage of life, while remaining free from attachment to their fruits. (2.51)
Men attached to sense objects, desiring pleasure within those very objects, have their liberation obstructed by words and persist in sinful action. (2.52)
Seeing the self by means of the self, one sees nothing whatsoever here;
at that time, in the total renunciation of action, there is no fault—this is my view. (2.53)
Desires and the like dissolve through knowledge alone and not otherwise; when all objective principles have ceased to exist, the reality itself shines forth spontaneously. (2.54)
The third chapter: Within the heart there is a divine lotus adorned with a divine liṅga, endowed with the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, and embellished by the twelve syllables. (3.1)
The vital breath (prāṇa) dwells right there, adorned with latent impressions (vāsanās), bound by beginningless karma, and having attained union with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). (3.2)
Due to the different modifications of the vital breath (prāṇa), there exist various names; it is simply impossible to recount them all. (3-3)
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna as the fifth;
nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. (3–4)
I have here in this scripture declared ten principal names;
impelled by their own respective functions, they perform their activities herein.
Here too, there are five principal winds, each of which is further divided into ten;
among those, I have declared the prāṇa and apāna to be the most excellent performers.
Prāṇa is in the heart; apāna is in the anus; samāna is in the region of the navel;
udāna resides in the region of the throat; and vyāna pervades the entire body. (3.7)
The five winds beginning with *nāga* perform [their functions] during the physical struggle;
they cause belching, opening the eyes, hunger, thirst, yawning, and hiccups as the fifth. (3-8)
He who indeed understands the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as a physical form according to this method, being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme goal. (3.9)
Now I shall speak for the swift accomplishment of yoga, so that yogins, having understood this, do not despair in the practice of yoga. (3.10)
Knowledge originating from the mouth of the Guru shall be possessed of power;
otherwise, it would be devoid of fruit, powerless, and a giver of great suffering. (3.11)
Those who, having diligently satisfied their guru, indeed practice the vidyā, shall obtain the fruit of that vidyā through its support. || 3-12 ||
The guru is the father, the guru is the mother, and the guru is the god; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, he is to be served in every way—by deed, by mind, and by speech. (3.13)
Through the grace of the guru, everything auspicious for oneself is obtained;
therefore, the guru should be served constantly, for otherwise no good will come to pass. (3.14)
Having performed three circumambulations and touched [the feet] with the left hand,
one should pay homage to the lotus-feet of the Guru with the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra).
For men who possess self-mastery and faith, accomplishment is certain;
for others, however, there will be no accomplishment. Therefore, one should strive to achieve it with diligence. (3-16)
It would not be [attained] by those possessed of doubt, nor likewise by those who are distrustful;
nor by those devoid of worship of the Guru, nor by those who have many attachments. (3.17)
And for those who delight in false speech, those who speak harshly, and those who lack devotion toward their guru, there shall never be any accomplishment. (3.17)
The conviction that "it will bear fruit" is the first sign of success;
the second is being endowed with faith, and the third is the worship of the guru.
The fourth is the state of equanimity; the fifth is the restraint of the senses;
the sixth is moderation in food; and the seventh does not exist at all. (3-18)
Having received instruction in yoga and found a teacher who knows yoga, one should practice it after determining the method taught by the teacher through the intellect. (3.19)
In a very beautiful hermitage, the yogi, assuming the lotus posture (padmāsana),
should sit upon his seat and practice the regulation of breath (pavanābhyāsa).
With body erect and palms joined in reverence, the wise one bows to his gurus;
then again, he salutes Vighneśa on the right and Kṣetrapāla and Ambikā on the left.
Then, having blocked the *piṅgalā* with the right thumb, the wise practitioner should fill the breath through the *iḍā* and retain it by means of *kumbhaka* according to his capacity.
Then, having abandoned it, Piṅgalā did so by means of her very food, and not with speed.
Again, having filled [the breath] through Piṅgalā, one should retain it according to one's capacity;
one should exhale the air through Iḍā slowly and gradually, not with force.
One should perform this twenty-fold breath-retention (kumbhaka) according to the rules of yoga, every day, free from all pairs of opposites and devoid of sloth. (3.24)
At dawn, at midday, at sunset, and at midnight—one should thus perform the *kumbhakas* four times during these periods. (3.25)
In this manner, one who is free from laziness should practice day by day for three months;
thereafter, the purification of the channels will certainly occur without delay. (3.26)
But when the purification of the channels has occurred for the yogin who perceives reality, then, with faults destroyed, the undertaking [of yoga] becomes possible. (3-27)
The signs of the yogin are seen in the body due to the purification of the channels;
all these limbs [of yoga] are now being described by me in brief. (3.28)
He has a symmetrical body, is fragrant, possesses beautiful luster, and achieves a melodious voice;
he is a fulfiller of undertakings, just as his familiarity [with them] may be.
The accomplishment in all yogas consists of those states of yoga. (3-29)
We have now described the preliminary practice for the sake of mastering the vital breath (vāyu);
hereafter, another method is taught which destroys the flood of all sufferings.
Possessing a mature digestive fire, enjoying excellent pleasures, happy, and beautiful in all his limbs;
with a full heart, the yogi is endowed with every enthusiasm and strength.
All of this necessarily arises within the body of the yogin. (3.31)
Now I shall declare that which is to be avoided, the supreme obstacle to yoga, by means of which yogins, having crossed the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra, shall proceed [to liberation]. (3.32)
Sour food, armpits, as well as pungent, salty, mustard-based, and spicy items;
excessive wandering, bathing at dawn, and the burning sensation caused by oil—these [are to be avoided].
Theft, violence, hatred of people, egoism, dishonesty, fasting [without purpose], untruthfulness, and the harming of living beings— [these he abandoned].
A yogi should certainly renounce these: attachment to women, service to fire, excessive talk, pleasant and unpleasant things, and eating to excess. (3.33)
And I shall proclaim the method for the swift accomplishment of yoga, which must be kept secret by practitioners so that success may indeed be attained. (3-34)
Ghee, milk, sweet food, betel leaf without lime,
camphor that is free of husk, sweet and well-matured, with fine pores.
Constantly listening to the established doctrine, dwelling in detachment from the household life,
chanting the names of Viṣṇu, and hearing the sublime sound [of his praise].
Fortitude, forbearance, austerity, purity, modesty, discernment, and service to the guru—a yogi should always practice these supreme observances. (3.35)
When the sun enters the wind, yogis should always eat;
when the moon has entered the wind, the best of practitioners should sleep. (3.36)
Even when one is hungry immediately after eating, the wise do not practice;
at the time of practice, one should first consume food consisting of milk and clarified butter. (3.37)
Then, once the practice has become firm, one should not maintain such strict observance of rules;
the practitioner should consume [food] in small quantities and in many different ways.
One should perform the *kumbhaka* breath-retentions every day at the time previously mentioned.
Then the yogin will possess the power to retain the breath as desired;
through retaining the breath at will, the practice of *kumbhaka* is certainly perfected.
When kevala-kumbhaka is mastered, what is there that cannot be achieved here for the yogin? (3.39)
Sweat arises on the body of the yogin during the first effort;
when sweat has arisen, the wise one should perform massage.
Otherwise, during the dissolution of the body, the yogin’s constituent elements perish. (3-40)
For in the second [stage] there may be trembling, while in the middle [stage] it is considered to be like that of a frog;
through practice even more intense than that, one becomes an achiever who travels through the sky. (3.41)
Even while seated in the lotus posture, the yogi exists having transcended the earth;
then that perfection of the vital air (vāyu-siddhi) should be known, which destroys the darkness of saṃsāra. (3.42)
For that duration, one should observe the restraints prescribed for yoga;
little sleep occurs, and only a small amount of feces and urine is produced.
For the yogi who perceives reality, there is health and freedom from dejection;
sweat, saliva, and worms do not arise in him under any circumstances whatsoever. (3.44)
At that time, the phlegm, bile, and wind within the body of the practitioner are in flux; therefore, the practitioner must observe no restrictive rules regarding food. (3-45)
Having consumed even very little food in many ways, that yogi indeed suffers no distress;
then, by the power of practice, the yogi attains the perfection of moving upon the earth (bhūcarī-siddhi).
Just as the movement of frogs occurs through the striking of their palms. || 3-46 ||
There are many obstacles here, terrible and difficult to ward off;
nevertheless, the yogi should accomplish [his goal] even if his life-breaths have reached his throat.
Then, seated in seclusion with his senses restrained, the practitioner should mutter the Praṇava for a long time as a means to destroy obstacles. (3-48)
By means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the wise practitioner will certainly destroy previously accumulated karmas as well as those arising in this world. (3.49)
A preeminent yogi destroys previously accumulated sins and various merits by means of sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). 3.50
One should burn the heaps of cotton-like sins with the fire of universal dissolution;
thereafter, being liberated from sin, one should subsequently destroy even merits.

Having indeed attained the eightfold sovereign powers through breath control (prāṇāyāma), the lord of yogis, having crossed the ocean of sin and merit, attains the state of wandering through the three worlds. (3.52)
Then, through the very sequence of practice, it shall become three *ghaṭikās*, by which the yogi will certainly attain all his desired perfections (*siddhis*). (3.53)
Mastery over speech, the power to move at will, as well as far-sightedness,
hearing from afar, subtle vision, and the ability to enter the bodies of others.
By anointing with feces and urine, gold becomes invisible;
likewise, all these things, as well as the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva), belong to the yogins. (3.54)
When the supreme state of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā) is attained through the practice of breath-control (pavana), then there is nothing in this wheel of saṃsāra that one cannot sustain. (3.55)

Because the vital breath (prāṇa), the downward breath (apāna), sound (nāda), the drop (bindu), the individual self (jīvātman), and the supreme self (paramātman) come together and form [it], it is therefore called "the jar" (ghaṭa). || 3.56 ||
When one is able to maintain [the breath] for even a single watch (yāma), then the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) becomes marvelous; it certainly does not occur before that. (3.57)
Whatever the lord of yogis knows, he should contemplate that as the Self;
by means of whichever senses [he perceives] their respective modes, there shall be mastery over those senses. (3.58)
When one *yāma* has been fully completed through the practice of yoga,
the yogi should then perform the *kumbhaka* once.
When the eight-fold staff (daṇḍāṣṭaka) becomes motionless for the yogin, then,
by his own power, the wise one should remain like a madman within the big toe.
Thereafter, through practice, the state of familiarity arises for the yogi when the vital breath (vāyu),
having abandoned the moon and the sun, remains motionless.
The wind becomes well-acquainted with the wind; the Suṣumnā moves within the void.
Having firmly grasped the power of action and having certainly pierced through the wheels,
when the state of mastery arises through the yoga of practice;
Then the yogi certainly perceives the three peaks of karmas. || 3-61 ||
Then, one should destroy the accumulations of karma with the *praṇava*;
that yogi may, for the sake of experiencing karma, perform the emanation of a multitude of bodies. (3.62)
At this time, the great yogi should practice fivefold concentration, by which the accomplishments beginning with the earth arise, and thereby the fear of the elements is dispelled. (3.63)
There are five *ghaṭikās* in the *ādhāra*, and likewise in the location of the *liṅga*;
above that, there are five *ghaṭikās* in the center of the *nābhi* and the *hṛdaya*.
Likewise, the wise one should hold [the breath] for five ghaṭikās above the space between the eyebrows;
thus, the lord of yogis shall certainly not be lost to the elements, beginning with the earth. (3.64)
The wise man who practices the retention of all beings—even if he dies after a hundred Brahmās, death does not exist for him. (3.65)
Then, through the very process of practice, the perfection of the yogi shall come to be;
by which he, having crossed over the seeds of karma from time immemorial, may drink the nectar of immortality. (3.66)
When the perfection of samādhi occurs through one's own practice,
it belongs to the wise yogi who is peaceful and liberated while living.
When the meditative absorption (samādhi) has reached perfection and occurs at will,
the powerful wind, having seized the volition and the capacity for action, [proceeds].
And having conquered all the wheels, it dissolves into the power of gnosis.
Now, for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions, the practice of the winds must be explained, by which the certain cessation of enjoyments within this wheel of saṃsāra will occur. (3-68)
The wise one who, having placed the tongue at the root of the palate, drinks the vital breath (prāṇānila), for him there shall be an exhaustion of all [worldly] yogas. (3.69)
The wise person who drinks the cool air with the beak of a crow,
knowing the method of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, shall become a vessel for liberation.
The wise practitioner who drinks the vital wind daily according to the prescribed rule—for that yogi, fatigue, fever, old age, and disease perish. (3.71)
Having directed the tongue upward, whoever drinks the water [of the moon], that lord of yogis will certainly conquer death within a single month. (3.72)
Having firmly pressed the space between the teeth according to the prescribed method and drinking [the nectar],
while meditating upon the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, one becomes a poet within six months.
One should drink air with the beak of a crow during both twilights, meditating on the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī for the pacification of the disease of consumption. (3.74)
Day and night, the wise yogi should drink with the "crow-beak" [technique];
by drinking the vital breath (prāṇānila), there shall be a complete destruction of his diseases.
Likewise, there shall indeed be the hearing of distant sounds, the seeing of distant forms, and true vision. (3.75)
Pressing his teeth against his teeth, the wise man should drink air very slowly with his tongue raised; thus he conquers death before long. (3.76)
He who practices this for even six months day after day becomes liberated from all sins and indeed destroys all diseases. (3.77)
Through practice performed for a year, one certainly becomes Bhairava;
having personally conquered the host of elements and attained the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest. (3.78)
If one holds the tongue upward for even half a moment, the yogi is liberated in an instant from disease, death, old age, and the like. (3.79)
One should contemplate the rasanā, conjoined with the vital breath, as being pressed;
for such a person death does not occur—this I have spoken as the truth, the absolute truth. (3.80)
Through such practice of yoga, one becomes a second Kāmadeva;
neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor even fainting occurs. (3.81)
By this very method, the lord of yogis shall become one who moves at will upon the circle of the earth, entirely free from all calamities.
There is no returning for him again; he rejoices even with the gods.
He is not stained by merit or sin, for he has attained this imperishable state.
There are eighty-four types of seats of various kinds;
having selected four from among them, I shall speak of those which I have taught.
Then [he should practice] Siddhāsana, Padmāsana, Ugrāsana, and Svastika. || 3-84 ||
The practitioner, exerting effort to press the perineum with the base of the foot,
should always place the base of the foot upon the penis, O knower of yoga.
Gazing upward at the space between the eyebrows, motionless, with senses restrained, the body held straight and free from agitation, he remains in solitude.
This is to be known as Siddhāsana, which bestows perfection upon the perfected ones.
By means of which one may quickly attain the perfection of yoga through the power of practice;
therefore, Siddhāsana should always be practiced by the supreme practitioner of breath control. (3.86)
By means of which one abandons saṃsāra and attains the supreme goal;
there exists no secret seat on earth more excellent than this.
By the mere act of meditating upon which, the yogi is liberated from sin. || 3-87 ||
Having carefully placed the two feet flat upon the thighs,
one should likewise place the two hands flat upon the middle of the thighs.
One should fix the gaze on the tip of the nose, place the tongue against the root of the teeth,
lift the chin toward the chest, and slowly raise the breath.
Having drawn [the breath] in as much as possible, one should slowly fill the abdomen;
then, according to one's capacity and without strain, one should exhale.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all diseases.
That which is difficult for anyone to attain is obtained by the wise person.
When the practice is performed, the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes even and steady at that very moment; for the practitioner who practices correctly, this will happen without a doubt. (3-90)
The yogi seated in the lotus posture, by means of the regulation of prāṇa and apāna, shall fill [the body]; he will become liberated—this I tell you as the truth, the absolute truth. (3.91)
Extending both feet so that they do not touch each other,
and firmly grasping them with both hands, one should place the head upon the knees.
This is declared to be the Āsanogram, which kindles the vital breath (anila) and removes the exhaustion of the body; it is known by the name Paścimottāna.
If a wise person practices this supreme posture every day, his vital breath (vāyu) will certainly circulate through the western path (the suṣumṇā). (3.92)
For those who practice this, all perfections arise;
therefore, the yogi should strive with effort to accomplish his own perfection. (3.93)
This must be guarded with great effort and not given to just anyone;
by means of it, the accomplishment of the Wind (Marutsiddhi) is swiftly attained, which destroys the flood of suffering. (3-94)
Holding both soles of the feet properly between the knees and the thighs, sitting comfortably with the body straight—this they call the Svastika posture. (3.95)
By this method, the wise yogi should master the vital air (māruta);
no disease shall affect his body, and the wind [element] becomes perfected for him. (3.96)
This is declared to be the comfortable posture (sukhāsana), which destroys all suffering;
it is the svastika, to be kept secret by yogis, the supreme bringer of well-being.
The Fourth Chapter:
At the outset, by means of the yoga of inhalation (pūraka), one should fill the mind in its own base (svādhāra).
By contracting the yoni located between the anus and the genitals, it is set in motion. (4-1)
Having meditated upon Kāma, who has entered the womb of Brahmā, resembling a ball,
radiant as ten million suns, and as cool as ten million moons;
Above that, however, is the subtle crest (śikhā), which is the supreme digit (kalā) whose nature is consciousness;
one should contemplate oneself as united and become one with it. (4.2)
He indeed proceeds by way of the path of Brahman through the sequence of the three marks;
for that is the nectar situated in heaven, characterized by supreme bliss.
White and red, rich with splendor, raining down streams of nectar—one who has drunk the divine *kulāmṛta* shall enter the *kula* once again. (4.3)
One should go to the family again by means of the mother, and not otherwise;
for she has been described by me in this tantra as being equal to one's own life-force.
Furthermore, everything from the fire of time (kālāgni) up to Śiva dissolves into that [source].
This indeed is the supreme Yonimudrā; its binding has been proclaimed.
By the mere binding of this [mudrā], there is nothing that it cannot accomplish. (4-5)
Those mantras whose forms are severed, those that are pinned down or paralyzed,
those mantras that are burnt, those lacking the crest-syllable (śikhā), those that are defiled, and those that have been cast aside;
The dull-witted, children, the elderly, those mature yet arrogant in their youth, those who stand on the side of the enemy, the powerless, those devoid of courage,
as well as those lacking fortitude and those who are broken and shattered into a hundred pieces.
When joined with the prescribed ritual procedure and applied by the Guru, they all swiftly become bestowers of both spiritual perfection and liberation.
Having initiated [the disciple] according to the rule and having consecrated him a thousandfold,
this mudrā is proclaimed for the purpose of conferring authority over the mantras.
Even if one were to commit thousands of Brahman-murders or destroy the three worlds, one is not tainted by sin through the binding of the Yoni-mudrā. (4.7)
One who kills a guru, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
by means of the binding of the *yonimudrā*, one shall not be bound by these sins.
Therefore, constant practice must be performed by those who desire liberation;
from practice comes perfection, and through practice one attains liberation. (4.9)
Through practice one attains consciousness; yoga proceeds from practice.
The perfection of the mudrās comes from practice, and the mastery of the vital winds comes from practice.
Through practice, there shall be deception of time, and likewise, one becomes a conqueror of death.
Through the yoga of practice, mastery of speech and the power to act according to one's will shall arise.
The *yonimudrā* is supremely secret and must not be given to just anyone;
it should never be imparted under any circumstances, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
Now I shall describe the supreme yoga that brings about the perfection of yoga, which is most difficult to obtain and must be kept secret even from those who have attained great siddhi. (4.12)
When Kuṇḍalī, who was asleep, awakens by the grace of the Guru,
then all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the application of mudrās to awaken the Goddess who is sleeping at the opening of the *brahmarandhra*. (4.14)
Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, Mahāvedha, and Khecarī; Jālandhara, Mūlabandha, and likewise Viparītakṛti.
Uḍḍāna, vajroṇī, and in the tenth, śakticālana—this indeed is the tenfold set of mudrās, the most excellent among all mudrās. (4.15)
Now follows the exposition of Mahāmudrā:
I shall proclaim Mahāmudrā in this tantra, which is dear to me—that having attained which the Siddhas of old, such as Kapila and others, reached perfection. (4-16)
Having respectfully pressed with the root of the foot using the left hand (apasavya),
according to the teacher’s instruction, [one should focus on] the yoni located between the anus and the penis.
Holding the outstretched left foot with both hands,
one should restrain the nine openings and place the chin upon the heart.
Having placed the mind upon the path of the mind, one should practice the sādhana of the vital wind;
this becomes Mahāmudrā, which is concealed in all the tantras.
Having practiced with the left limb, the yogi of restrained mind, having performed the breath control equally, should practice again with the right limb. (4.17)
By this method, even a yogi of meager fortune attains success;
it consists of the movement of all the *nāḍīs* and the cessation of the *bindu*.
Indeed, this decoction is a life-sustainer, a destroyer of sins,
a pacifier of all diseases, and an increaser of the digestive fire.
It bestows upon the body stainless luster, destroys old age and death,
grants the fruits of desired objects, provides happiness, and brings about the subduing of the senses.
All these have been declared for the yogi who has ascended to yoga; through practice, they will certainly come to pass—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (4.18)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, this mudrā must be guarded with great effort;
for by attaining it, yogins go to the further shore of the ocean of existence. (4.19)
This mudrā, which is like a wish-granting cow for practitioners, has been taught by me;
it should be performed with secret conduct and must not be given to just anyone. (4-20)
Now, the description of Mahābandha:
Then, having extended one leg and placed it upon the thigh,
contracting the anus and the *yoni*, and drawing the *apāna* upward;
Having joined [the breath] with the equal [breath], one should make the vital air face downward.

The wise one who binds [the breath] with the prāṇa and apāna for the sake of upward movement— this is called the Great Lock (mahābandha), which bestows the path to perfection. Through it, the flow of vital essence from the network of channels reaches the head of the yogi.
One should accomplish it with both feet, each with great effort.
Through practice, the vital air (vāyu) becomes firmly established within the Suṣumnā;
by this, there is nourishment of the body and firm binding of the skeletal frame.
The yogi becomes one whose heart is completely fulfilled;
by this bond, O lord of yogis, the yogi shall accomplish everything desired.
Now, the description of the Great Piercing (Mahāvedha):
O Mistress of the Three Worlds, having brought about the union of the Apāna and Prāṇa breaths,
the yogi established in the Great Piercing fills his belly with air.
The wise man should strike the two buttocks; this is proclaimed by me as the piercing (vedha).
Having pierced with this piercing, that bull among yogis pierces the knot of Brahma at the path of the Suṣumṇā by means of the vital air (vāyu). || 4.24 ||
For one who constantly practices the well-guarded Great Piercing (mahāvedha), there shall arise the perfection of the vital wind (vāyusiddhi) which destroys old age and death. (4-25)
The gods situated within the wheel tremble from the blow of the wind;
even Kuṇḍalī, the Great Māyā, dissolves into Kailāsa.
The great seal (mahāmudrā) and the great bond (mahābandha) are fruitless when devoid of piercing (vedha);
therefore, the yogi should diligently perform the triad in succession. (4-27)
He who performs these three with diligence four times [daily] undoubtedly conquers death within six months; of this there is no doubt. (4.28)
A perfected one (siddha), and no other, knows the majesty of this triad;
having known it, all practitioners indeed attain perfect accomplishment (siddhi). || 4-29 ||
It must be guarded with great effort by practitioners desiring accomplishment;
otherwise, there will be no success—this is the certain conclusion regarding the mudrās.
Now follows the description of the Khecarī Mudrā:
Having fixed his gaze firmly between the two eyebrows, the wise man,
seated upon the Vajra posture, free from various disturbances, [should practice].
The wise practitioner should diligently join the tongue, turned upward, into the cavity situated above the uvula within the well of nectar;
this is declared to be the Khecarī Mudrā for the sake of devoted followers. (4.31)
For she is the mother of all spiritual accomplishments and is dearer to me than my own life;
by practicing her continuously, one should drink nectar every day.
By that, the accomplishment of the body occurs; he is the lion to the elephant of death. (4.32)
Whether impure or pure, even if one has reached every possible state, he whose khecarī is purified is truly pure; of this there is no doubt. (4.33)
He who spends even half a moment [in this practice] after having crossed the great ocean of sin,
shall enjoy divine pleasures and be reborn into a noble family.
This is the Khecarī mudrā; he who, with a steady mind and free from sloth, perceives even half a moment as the passing of a hundred Brahmās.
The wise person who, through the instruction of the guru, knows this Khecarī Mudrā, even if he is engaged in various sins, attains the supreme goal. (4.36)
This mudrā, which is like one's own life-breath, is not to be given to just anyone;
this mudrā must be carefully concealed, O Goddess worshipped by the gods. (4.37)
Now, the Jālandhara-bandha:
Having bound the network of vessels in the throat, one should place the chin upon the heart;
this is declared to be the Jālandhara-bandha, difficult even for the gods to attain.
The fire residing in the navel of living beings drinks the expansion of nectar falling from the thousand-petaled lotus; for that purpose, one should perform this binding.
By means of this bond, the wise one drinks nectar himself;
and having attained immortality, he rejoices in the three worlds. (4.39)
This is the Jālandhara-bandha, which bestows success upon the perfected ones;
it should be practiced constantly by the yogi who desires accomplishment. (4.40)
Now, the root-lock (mūlabandha):
Having firmly compressed the anal passage with the heel of the foot and well-restrained,
one should forcefully draw up the apāna wind and gradually move it upward.
This imagined root-binding destroys old age and death.
By means of this bond, one brings about the supreme unification of the downward-moving breath (apāna) and the upward-moving breath (prāṇa); through this, the Yonimudrā is thoroughly perfected. (4.42)
When the *yonimudrā* is perfected, what on this earth is not accomplished?
By the grace of this *bandha*, one surpasses even the gods in the sky.
Seated in the lotus posture, the yogi remains, having abandoned the earth.
A preeminent yogi who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra should practice this binding in a well-concealed and solitary place. (4-44)
Now, the mudrā that performs the reversal:
Having placed one's head upon the ground, one should lead both feet into the sky.
This is the "performer of the reversal," hidden in all tantras. (4.45)
The yogi who practices this constantly for even a single watch (yāma) conquers death; he does not perish even at the time of universal dissolution.
He who drinks the nectar [of the teachings] shall attain equality with the Siddhas;
he who binds this [disciple] is to be served by all the worlds.
One should perform the backward expansion (tāna) both above and below the navel;
this is the Uḍḍiyāna Bandha, which destroys the flood of all suffering.
One should perform the final contraction in the abdomen above the navel;
this is the bandha called Uḍḍiyāna, the lion that destroys the elephant of death. (4.48)
If a yogi performs this constantly four times every day,
the navel becomes purified, whereby the vital breath (marut) becomes perfected.
The yogi who practices for six months certainly conquers death;
his digestive fire blazes and an increase in vital essence (rasa) occurs.
By this, the accomplishment of the body is produced even more effectively;
furthermore, the destruction of diseases certainly occurs for the yogin. (4.51)

Having received [the instruction] from the guru with diligent effort, the wise one should practice it in a secluded and well-situated place—the supreme binding that is exceedingly difficult to attain. (4.52)
Now, the Śakticālana-mudrā:
The wise one should rouse the firm Kuṇḍalinī, who is sleeping in the Ādhāra-lotus,
having forcefully drawn her upward by mounting upon the apāna-vāyu.
This is the Śakticālana-mudrā, which bestows all powers. || 4-53 ||
For he who practices the movement of the *śakti* in this manner every day, there shall be an increase in lifespan and the destruction of diseases. (4-54)
Having abandoned sleep, the serpent-like slumber shall indeed rise up by itself;
therefore, an ascetic desiring perfection must practice this posture. 4-55.
For one who constantly practices the supreme *śakticālana*, by which the perfection of the body (*vigrahasiddhi*)— which bestows qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest—
is attained, how can there be any fear of death according to the method of the Guru’s instruction? (4-56)

For one who diligently performs the movement of the *śakti* according to the prescribed method for a duration of two *muhūrtas*, success is not far off. The yogis should perform the movement of the *śakti* while remaining in a steady posture. (4–57)
This tenfold set of mudrās has not existed in the past, nor will it exist in the future;
success is achieved through the practice of each one individually—it is not otherwise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Mudrās," in the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī within the venerable Śivasaṃhitā. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
Speak these words to me, O Lord, regarding the wisdom of the ultimate truth;
tell me, O beloved Śaṅkara, what obstacles exist for the worlds. (5.1)
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain how obstacles always stand in the way of men's liberation; for worldly enjoyment is the supreme bondage. (5.2)
Now begins the description of the obstacles to the yoga of the form of enjoyment:
women, beds, seats, clothing, and wealth are but a mockery for him; likewise are betel, food, vehicles, and the splendors of royal power and sovereignty.
Gold, silver, copper, gems, aguru, and cows;
scholarship, the Vedic scriptures, dance, song, and ornaments;
the flute, the lute, clay drums, the lordly elephant, and the horse-vehicle.
Wives, children, and sense objects—these are proclaimed to be obstacles;
these obstacles take the form of enjoyments. Now hear about those that take the form of dharma.
Now follows the description of the obstacles to the yoga of the nature of Dharma:
bathing, the ritual of worship, fire-offerings, as well as the state consisting of liberation,
vows, fasting, observances, silence, and the restraint of the senses.
Meditation upon the object of worship, as well as the meditation itself, the mantra, charity, and fame throughout the quarters;
the construction of step-wells, wells, tanks, palaces, and groves;
sacrifice, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, the Kṛcchra penance, and various sacred pilgrimage sites.
And these obstacles are seen existing in the form of the Dharma. || 5-4 ||
Now, the description of the obstacles to the nature of knowledge: O fair-faced one, I shall describe that obstacle which exists within knowledge;
having made the cow’s mouth one’s own seat, and having performed the cleansing of *dhauti*.

The consciousness of the movement through the channels, the cessation of sensory withdrawal, the rapid shifting within the belly, and entry through the path of the senses—these are the auspicious functions of the channels; now listen to my teaching on nourishment. 5-5.
One should cut the nine-fold mineral juice and strike it with ginger;
by practicing this at one time, meditative absorption (*samādhi*) will arise—listen to this which has become the very mark of attainment.
Seek the company of the virtuous and maintain a sense of restraint toward the wicked;
one should observe the movement of the breath as it enters and exits like a heavy watchman. (5.7)
"Piṇḍastha, Rūpasaṃstha, Rūpastha, and Rūpavarjita—this is Brahman within this state of mind, and the heart becomes tranquil.
Thus have these obstacles been described, which are established in the form of knowledge. (5–8)
Now, the exposition of the fourfold yoga:
Mantrayoga, Haṭhayoga, and Layayoga as the third;
the fourth is Rājayoga, which is devoid of dualistic states. (5.9)
The practitioner should be known as fourfold: the weak, the middling, the superior, and the most superior;
the most superior is the best, for he is capable of leaping across the ocean of existence. (5.10)
Now, the characteristics of the inferior practitioner:
one who lacks enthusiasm, is utterly deluded, afflicted by disease, a reviler of the guru,
greedy, evil-minded, gluttonous, and dependent on women.
One who is fickle, cowardly, diseased, dependent on others,
excessively cruel, of poor conduct, and of weak vigor should be known as a person of mild nature.
In twelve years, supreme accomplishment will arise for him through diligent effort;
he should certainly be recognized by the Guru as one qualified for the yoga of mantra. (5.11)
Possessing equanimity, endowed with patience, desiring merit, and speaking kindly—
one who is impartial in all undertakings will undoubtedly become common to all.
Knowing this very thing, the gurus bestow liberation through absorption.
Now, the characteristics of the practitioner of superior capacity:
one who possesses steady intelligence, is disciplined in dissolution, is self-reliant, and is also endowed with vigor;
who is magnanimous, compassionate, patient, and truthful as well.
One who is heroic, in the prime of youth, possessed of faith, a worshiper of the lotus feet of the guru,
and devoted to the practice of yoga— such a person is to be known as one of superior capacity (adhimātraka).
The accomplishment of this [practice] shall occur within six years through the application of practice;
to such a steadfast person, Haṭhayoga is bestowed along with its auxiliary limbs. (5.13)
Now, the characteristics of one who accomplishes the highest degree [of success]:
endowed with great vigor and enthusiasm, pleasing, and even heroic;
knowledgeable in the treatises, habituated to practice, free from delusion, and undisturbed.
Endowed with fresh youth, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses,
he was fearless, pure, skillful, a giver of gifts, and a refuge for all people.
The qualified practitioner is steadfast, wise, remaining as he pleases, and patient;
he is of good character, a follower of dharma, one whose actions are concealed, and who speaks kindly.
Endowed with faith in the scriptures, worshipping the deities and the guru,
detached from the company of worldly people, and free from major diseases.
And for one who observes the vows intensely and accomplishes all yoga, success is achieved within three years; of this there is no doubt.
He is entitled to all yogas; no deliberation is required in this matter.
Now, the meditation on symbols (pratīkopāsana).
Meditation on symbols should be performed, as it bestows both visible and invisible fruits;
it purifies by the mere sight [of the symbol]. There is no need for deliberation on this point. (5-15)
When, in the intense heat, he beholds the Lord reflected in his own image with eyes wide open,
and looks toward the sky, he sees at that very moment his own reflection in the courtyard of the heavens.
For one who indeed beholds their own reflection daily in the courtyard of the sky, there shall be an increase in lifespan; death shall never occur for them. (5.17)
When he sees his own reflection complete within the courtyard of the sky, then he attains victory and may move about having conquered the wind. (5.18)
He who constantly practices and worships the Supreme Self—the singular Person of perfect bliss—through the grace of his own icon. (5.19)
During a journey, at the time of marriage, during an auspicious rite, in times of distress,
for the destruction of sin, and for the increase of merit, one should perform the worship of the image.
Through uninterrupted practice, the yogi of restrained mind certainly perceives [the Self] within; then he attains liberation. (5.21)
One should firmly block both ears with the two thumbs, the two eyes with the two index fingers,
the two nostrils with the two middle fingers, and the mouth with the two ring fingers.
When the yogi completely restrains the vital breath, he then perceives the Self as a characteristic mark in the form of light. (5.22)
He by whom that light is seen for even a moment without distraction, being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme goal. (5.23)
The yogi, having practiced continuously and being freed from all impurities, forgets the entire body and so forth, and having become non-different from That, he has himself gone [to That]. (5.24)
That person who always practices with secret conduct shall indeed be dissolved into Brahman, even if they are devoted to sinful actions. (5.25)
This yoga of mine, which produces immediate conviction, bestows liberation upon the world, and is dear to me, must be guarded with great effort.
Indeed, through gradual practice, the *nāda* (inner sound) arises for him.
The first sound is like that of bees, flutes, and lutes;
through such practice, it subsequently destroys the darkness of saṃsāra.
Afterwards, the sound is like the ringing of a bell and resembles the roar of thunder;
when one remains fearless, having fixed the mind upon that sound.
Then, O beloved of mine, that dissolution arises for him.
In that regard, when the mind of the yogin takes great delight in the sound (nāda), forgetting everything external, it becomes tranquil along with the sound. (5.28)
Having conquered many virtues through the practice of this yoga,
and having renounced all undertakings, one dissolves into the space of consciousness.
There is no posture equal to Nāsana, no strength equal to Kumbhaka;
there is no Mudrā equal to Khecarī, and no dissolution (laya) equal to Nāda. (5.30)
Now, O beloved, I shall describe the experience of the liberated one, knowing which even a practitioner joined with sin attains liberation. (5-31)
Having properly worshipped the Lord and having perfectly performed the supreme yoga, the wise man, remaining well-composed, should receive [the initiation] after having satisfied his guru. (5.32)
Having offered all things, beginning with one's own life, and having thoroughly satisfied the teacher who knows yoga with great effort, this yoga is received by the wise. (5.33)
Having gratified the Brahmins and being endowed with various auspicious rites, the wise man,
having become pure, should receive the auspicious [image] in my abode.
Having renounced his former body and so forth by this method, the yogin, having assumed a divine form, should take up that which is about to be described. (5.35)
The yogi, seated in the lotus posture and avoiding the company of people, should block the two channels of consciousness with his two fingers. (5.36)
Then, from that [state], the stainless one, whose nature is bliss, manifests as accomplishment;
therefore, effort must be exerted toward that by which one shall indeed become accomplished. (5.37)
For one who constantly practices, accomplishment is not far off;
mastery over the vital winds (vāyu) will arise for him through this very sequence, without a doubt. (5.38)
If a yogi performs this even once, he will certainly destroy a flood of sins;
for him, the entry of the middle wind will occur—of this there is no doubt. (5.39)
The yogi who is habituated to this practice is honored by the gods;
having attained the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he may wander through the three worlds. (5.40)
Whatever form arises for him through the practice of the vital breath (anila), that form he assumes;
the wise man, established in the Self and united with it, sports intensely. (5.41)
This supreme yoga is to be kept strictly secret and must not be given to just anyone;
it is certainly taught only to one who is endowed with the authoritative means of knowledge. 5-42.

When the yogi remains in the lotus posture (padmāsana) while recollecting [the breath] at the hollow of the throat (kaṇṭhakūpa), and having placed the tongue at the root of the palate (tālu), hunger and thirst cease. (5.43)
Below the pit of the throat, there is an auspicious channel called Kūrma;
by fixing the mind upon that, the yogi attains great stability of consciousness. (5.44)
When one meditates upon the cavity of the Rudrākṣa within the skull,
then a light will manifest with a radiance equal to a mass of lightning;
by the mere act of this meditation, the destruction of sins occurs.
Even a man of wicked conduct attains the supreme state.
When that wise person contemplates this day and night, he will certainly obtain the vision and the speech of the Siddhas. (5.46)
Standing, walking, sleeping, or eating, one should meditate on the void day and night;
then the yogi, composed of space, dissolves into the sky of consciousness. 5-47
This knowledge must always be practiced by a yogi desiring perfection;
through uninterrupted practice, he will certainly become equal to me.
By the power of this knowledge, the yogi becomes beloved by all. || 5-48 ||
Having conquered all beings, free from desire and without possessions,
he indeed beholds [the Self] at the tip of his nose while seated in the lotus posture.
Upon the death of the mind, his attainment of the power of moving through space (khecaratva) is accomplished. || 5-49 ||
The lord of yogis perceives the pure light, which is like a stainless mountain;
by the power of practice therein, he himself becomes its protector. (5.50)
Having slept on the ground on his back and meditating without interruption,
the wise yogi himself attains the immediate destruction of fatigue;
moreover, by meditating with his head toward the western direction, he becomes a conqueror of death.
Indeed, another [type of practitioner] is proclaimed as one who merely fixes his gaze between the eyebrows. || 5.51 ||
The essence of the four kinds of food is divided into three parts;
among these, that which is most substantial nourishes the subtle body (liṅgadeha).
Situated in the middle, it goes toward and nourishes this mass composed of the seven elements.
The third [element] goes outside after seven days in the form of feces and urine.
All those channels (nāḍīs) mentioned in the first two sections nourish the bodily wind from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. (5.53)
When the vital air (vāyu) circulates through all these channels, then the essence of food flows evenly throughout the body. (5.54)
Among those fourteen, ten here primarily participate in the activity;
they are the channels for the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), devoid of intensity. (5.55)
Two finger-breadths above the anus and one finger-breadth below the penis,
there exists the kanda, which is equal and measures four finger-breadths in its evenness.
The womb is oriented toward the west, situated between the anus and the genitals;
there the *kanda* is said to be located, and within it resides Kuṇḍalinī at all times.
Having coiled around all the channels, which are shaped like three and a half coils, she places her tail in the mouth and remains situated within the opening of the Suṣumṇā.
For this Goddess of Speech, known as the Seed-syllable, is like a sleeping serpent, quivering with her own radiance; she resides within the joints like a snake. (5.58)
This power of Viṣṇu should be known as a golden-lustrous waterfall, which gives birth to the three qualities: sattva, rajas, and tamas. (5.59)
In that regard, the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) is proclaimed to have the luster of a bandhūka flower; when employed in yoga, it takes the form of a letter resembling refined gold. (5-60)
The Suṣumṇā is also closely joined there, and the excellent seed is situated therein;
this radiance, resembling the autumnal moon, remains shining by itself.
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons—
when these three are united, she is the Goddess Tripurabhairavī.
That supreme splendor is proclaimed to be known as the seed-syllable (bīja). || 5-61 ||
Endowed with the powers of action and consciousness, it revolves all around;
from it rises a subtle water, red-tipped and rising in two hundred [streams].
That supreme splendor, established in the womb, is known as the Svayambhū-liṅga.
This is indeed the foundational lotus, whose source is the *kanda*;
it has four petals marked with the four letters beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*, which are quivering. (5.63)
The place called Kulā is golden-hued and joined with a self-manifested liṅga;
there the Siddha Dviraṇḍa resides, and there the deity is Ḍākinī.
The womb (yoni) is situated in the center of that lotus; there resides Kuṇḍalinī.
Above her is the seed-syllable of Kāma, a throbbing light, considered to be in constant motion.
For that wise one who constantly practices meditation in the *mūlādhāra*,
there shall indeed arise the accomplishment (*siddhi*) known as *dārdurī* through the process of abandoning the earth element.
An excellent luster of the body arises, as does the stimulation of the digestive fire; health, mental acuity, and omniscience are likewise produced. (5-65)

He knows everything—past, present, and future—together with its causes; he certainly becomes one who possesses all the scriptures, even those not heard before, along with their secret doctrines. (5-66)
The goddess Sarasvatī always dances intensely within his mouth;
through mere recitation, he shall attain mastery over mantras—of this there is no doubt. (5–67)
The word of the Guru destroys the flood of suffering consisting of old age and death.
This supreme meditation must always be practiced by one who trains in breath-control (pavana).
By meditation alone, the lord of yogis is liberated from all taints. (5–68)
When the yogi meditates upon the root-lotus, which is the self-arisen liṅga, then at that very moment he will certainly destroy the flood of his sins. (5-69)
Whatever one desires in the mind, that very fruit one shall obtain;
through uninterrupted practice, one beholds Him who bestows liberation.
It is the most excellent, both externally and internally, and should be worshipped with great effort;
for this is the very best of all, and in my opinion, there is nothing else superior to it.

He who, having abandoned Śiva who resides within himself, worships him as existing outside, is like one who casts away the food-ball held in his own hand and wanders about in search of sustenance. (5.71)
One should perform the worship of the self’s emblem every day without indolence;
for such a person, all success shall be attained—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (5.72)
Through uninterrupted practice for six months, one shall attain perfection;
the entry of the vital air (vāyu) into the suṣumṇā will certainly occur for such a person. (5.73)
And one attains mastery over the mind through the retention of the *vāyubindu*;
success in both this world and the next will surely come to pass—of this there is no doubt. (5.74)
Now follows the exposition of the Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra:
The second lotus is situated at the base of the linga;
it consists of six petals, is brilliantly radiant, and possesses the six syllables beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*.
That lotus known as Svādhiṣṭhāna is red in form;
there resides the Siddha named Bāla, and there resides the Goddess Rākiṇī.
He always meditates upon his own divine lotus of self-consecration;
all the women who are the limbs of desire, infatuated by passion, attend upon him. (5.76)
And having heard various scriptures not previously heard, he will certainly become free from doubt;
liberated from all diseases, he wanders in the world without fear. (5.77)
Death devours him, yet he is not devoured by anyone;
for him there shall be the supreme accomplishment that bestows the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
The vital air circulates within the body, and the increase of the vital essence (rasa) occurs with certainty;
even the nectar dripping from the sky-lotus increases. (5.78)
Now, the exposition of the Maṇipūra-cakra:
The third lotus, located at the navel, is known as Maṇipūra; it has ten spokes, is adorned with the letters from 'ḍa' to 'pha', and is golden in color. (5.79)
Where the Siddha named Rudra resides, the bestower of all auspiciousness, there dwells the goddess named Lākinī, who is supremely righteous. (5.80)
In that Maṇipūraka, the yogi always performs meditation;
for him, there arises the attainment of Pātāla, which brings constant bliss.
And that which is desired in this world—the destruction of suffering and disease, the deception of Time (Death), and even the entry into another's body—[shall be attained]. (5.81)
