The creation of gold from the Jāmbūnada river and other substances occurs, as does the vision of the Siddhas;
there shall also be the vision of medicinal herbs and the vision of hidden treasures. || 5.82 ||
In the heart, there is the fourth lotus, named Anāhata;
it is the locus of the phonemes from Ka to Tha and is endowed with twelve spokes.
The seed-syllable of Vāyu, which is deep red, is said to be the locus of clarity.
That supreme splendor situated upon a lotus is celebrated as the Bāṇaliṅga;
by the mere remembrance of which one obtains the fruits of both the seen and the unseen worlds. (5.84)
Where the Siddha Pinākin resides, and where the deity Kākinī dwells—
in that very heart-lotus, he who constantly performs meditation.
Indeed, his beloved celestial women, afflicted by desire, become agitated.
His knowledge shall be incomparable and have the three times as its object; he possesses the power of hearing from afar and seeing from afar, and he may travel through the air at will. (5.86)
There shall be the vision of the Siddhas and likewise the vision of the Yoginīs;
there shall be the attainment of moving through the sky (khecarasiddhi) and the victory over those who move through the sky.
He who constantly meditates upon the supreme second Bāṇaliṅga shall attain the siddhis of Khecarī and Bhūcarī; of this there is no doubt. (5.88)
The greatness of this meditation cannot indeed be described;
even all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, keep this secret. (5.89)
Now, the explanation of the Viśuddha-cakra:
The lotus situated in the region of the throat is the fifth, named Viśuddha;
it has the luster of fine gold, is endowed with vowels, and is joined with the sixteen vowels.
Chagalāṇḍa is the perfected one (siddha) here, and Śākinī is the presiding deity.
He who constantly practices meditation is a wise master of yoga;
however, for this yogin, [the practice] occurs elsewhere, in the lotus known as Viśuddha.
The four Vedas, along with their secret portions, shine forth like a treasure-trove. || 5-91 ||
When the yogi situated in the place of solitude becomes subject to anger, then the entire triple world trembles; of this there is no doubt. (5.92)
When, by the power of destiny or other causes, the mind of one becomes utterly dissolved in this state, then, having abandoned the external, it certainly delights within itself. (5.93)
Even in a thousand years, his own body—though as hard as a thunderbolt—does not suffer any injury due to its inherent power. (5.94)
When that lord of yogis abandons that meditation upon the surface of the earth,
the virtuous one considers those thousands of years as if they were a single moment.
Now, the exposition of the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*).
The lotus of command is between the eyebrows, possessing two petals and endowed with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*.
It has a white luster; there, Mahākāla is the perfected one (*siddha*), and the goddess is Hākinī. (5.96)
There, the seed-syllable (bīja), resembling the autumnal moon, has blossomed;
knowing this Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa) as the Person (Puruṣa), one does not perish. (5.97)
This alone is the supreme power of the mantra-practitioner in all tantras;
having contemplated this, one attains the highest accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.
The fourth is the triad of signs; I am that, the bestower of liberation.
Merely by meditating upon it, the lord of yogis certainly becomes equal to me. (5.99)
For Iḍā is known as Piṅgalā, and she is called Varaṇā;
Vārāṇasī is between those two, and Viśvanātha is said to be here.
The greatness of this sacred field has been proclaimed in many ways by seers who perceive the truth; it is the supreme reality, well-expounded in the scriptures. (5.101)
The Suṣumṇā has gone to Meru because it leads to the Brahma-randhra;
from there, it turns back and enters the right side of the lotus of the Command (ājñā).
It enters the left nostril and is celebrated as the Gaṅgā.

For that thousand-petaled lotus which is situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there is a source (yoni) within its bulb (kanda); therein the Moon is situated. From its triangular form, nectar flows continuously.
In the iḍā there is nectar; therein the moon flows evenly.
It carries nectar in a stream, a continuous flow in the form of a stream.
It enters the left nostril; indeed, it is called the Gaṅgā by the yogis. || 5.103 ||
Flowing from the right shoulder of the lotus of command toward the left nostril and moving upward, that channel is called Iḍā; it is designated as Varaṇā. (5.104)
Then, one should contemplate Vārāṇasī between those two;
Piṅgalā, having that same form, is within the lotus of its command.
"It indeed moves through the right nostril; thus has it been declared by us. (5.105)
Indeed, at the mūlādhāra there is a four-petalled lotus situated;
in its center is the womb (yoni), and within that, the sun is situated. (5.106)
From that solar orb, poison flows continuously;
there, the Sun deposits the poison into the Piṅgalā. (5.107)
That which flows there continuously in the form of a stream as poison proceeds through the right nostril; this is to be visualized as before. (5.108)
Having departed from the left petal of the lotus of command and entered the right nostril, the Piṅgalā, flowing upwards, was likewise proclaimed to have existed in the past. (5.109)
This is declared to be the Lotus of Command (Ājñāpadma), where the Lord Maheśvara resides;
above that, the three seats (pīṭha-traya) are described by those who contemplate yoga.
That which is called bindu, nāda, and śakti is situated in the lotus of the forehead.
Whoever constantly performs meditation upon the secret lotus of the Command, the karma created in previous births shall perish without obstruction. (5.111)
When the yogi, established here, practices meditation continuously,
then he performs image-worship and recitation as if they were useless.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, hosts of apsarases, and kinnaras—
all serve his feet, for they are all subject to his will.
The yogi makes the tongue enter [the cavity] and move in reverse;
having held it in the cavities above the uvula, he performs meditation that removes fear.
If one’s mind remains unshakable in this place for even half a moment, all of one’s sins go to destruction at that very instant. (5.114)
For whatever fruits have indeed been proclaimed regarding the five lotuses,
all of those certainly come about through this knowledge.
The wise one who always practices this command within the lotus, having cast aside the great bondage of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), rejoices. (5.116)
The wise person who, at the time of the departure of the vital breaths, leaves their life while remembering that lotus—that righteous soul merges into the Supreme Self. (5.117)
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, or waking, the man who practices meditation,
even while performing sinful deeds, does not sink into the mire of evil.
The yogi, completely liberated from bondage by his own radiance,
cannot possibly describe the greatness of the meditation on the two petals.
Even the deities beginning with Brahmā know only a small portion of me.
Above this, at the root of the palate, there is a thousand-petaled lotus where the base of the suṣumṇā remains with its opening. (5.120)
At the root of the palate, that Suṣumṇā proceeds with its opening downward;
in the Mūlādhāra, all the channels are situated, established within the yoni.
They are the seeds of reality and the bestowers of the path to Brahman.
And in the location of the palate, there is a thousand-spoked lotus established from of old;
at its bulb (kanda) there is a single yoni, which is considered to face westward.
In the center of that Suṣumṇā, the root remains with an opening;
that very place, from the lotus of the Mūlādhāra up to it, is called the Brahma-randhra.
Then, in that opening, her power—the Suṣumṇā, who is always Kuṇḍalinī—resides;
O beloved of mine, the power within the Suṣumṇā is eternally variegated.
In my view, the conceptualization of the *brahmarandhra* and so forth should be performed within that [channel]. (5.124)
By the mere recollection of her, the knowledge of Brahman arises, sins are destroyed, and a person shall not be born again. (5.125)
One should place the inserted moving big toe into one's own mouth;
by that means, the wind moving within the body does not flow out at all. (5.126)
Because of that, one wanders perpetually within this wheel of saṃsāra;
therefore, yogīs do not exert themselves for the mere maintenance of the vital breath (prāṇa).
For that very reason, all the channels (nāḍī) are obstructed and the eightfold encircling occurs.
This Kuṇḍalinī power does not leave the aperture otherwise.
When the channels are full and the vital breaths are completely restrained, then, by the release of the *bandhas*, the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī shall emerge from the aperture. (5.128)
This vital breath (prāṇasamīraṇa) should always flow within the Suṣumṇā;
the Yoni situated in the root-lotus is located at the left and right corners.
Between the iḍā and piṅgalā, the suṣumṇā resides in the center of the womb.
The aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is located right there within the sphere that is the support of the Suṣumṇā;
he who knows this, the discerning one, shall be liberated from the bondage of karma. || 5.130 ||
Their confluence occurs undoubtedly at the opening of the *brahmarandhra*;
for those who have performed their ablutions (*snātaka*), liberation shall result from bathing there without obstruction. (5.131)
This Sarasvatī flows between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā;
having bathed at their confluence, the fortunate man goes to the supreme goal.
In ancient times, Iḍā was said to be the Gaṅgā and Piṅgalā the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā);
the middle channel was called Sarasvatī, and the confluence of these three is exceedingly rare.
Whoever performs a mental bath at the confluence of the white and dark [rivers] is liberated from all sins and goes to the eternal Brahman.
Whoever performs the rites for the ancestors at the confluence of the Triveṇī indeed delivers all his ancestors and goes to the supreme goal.
He who performs daily, occasional, and optional rites every day after having reflected upon them with his mind shall obtain inexhaustible fruit.
He who performs the ritual bath even once enjoys happiness in heaven;
having indeed burnt away all sins without exception, that yogi becomes pure-minded himself.
Whether impure or pure, or even having fallen into any state whatsoever, one becomes purified merely by performing the ritual bath; it is not otherwise.
When at the time of death one contemplates the body as submerged in the waters of the Triveṇī and gives up the vital breaths, one shall then attain liberation.
There exists no secret more supreme than this in the three worlds;
it must be guarded with great effort and never disclosed at any time.
If one places the mind in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and remains there for even half a moment, being liberated from all sins, he attains the supreme goal. || 5.141 ||
The yogi whose mind is dissolved in Me merges into Me;
having enjoyed the powers such as *aṇimā* and others according to his own will, he becomes the Supreme Person. (5.142)
By the mere meditation upon this aperture, that mortal shall become dear to me in this saṃsāra;
having conquered sin, he becomes entitled to the path of liberation, and by bestowing knowledge, he truly delivers [others] in a wondrous way. (5-143)
Inaccessible to the gods, beginning with the four-faced Brahmā, and beloved by yogis—that Brahmarandhra, which must be carefully and secretly guarded, has been described by me. (5.144)
The lotus-source which was previously described by me as being in the thousand-petaled [cakra], beneath it resides the moon; that is the meditation performed by the wise. (5.145)
By the mere remembrance of whom, the lord of yogis becomes worthy of worship by the gods upon the circle of the earth and becomes esteemed by the perfected ones (siddhas). (5.146)
One should meditate on the great ocean as being burnt within the cavity of the skull;
situated there, one should contemplate the moon within the thousand-petaled lotus.
Within the cavity of the skull, endowed with sixteen digits (kalās),
one should contemplate that stainless [reality] known as the Moon of Nectar and the Swan;
through uninterrupted practice, one will certainly behold it within three days.
By the mere sight [of him], that practitioner indeed burns away the flood of sins. || 5.148 ||
It vibrates even into the future, and the purity of mind will surely arise;
having performed it immediately, it burns away even the five great sins. (5.149)

All the planets become favorable, all calamities perish, and afflictions are pacified; one shall obtain victory in battle. Through the sight of Kṣīra and Indu, the siddhis of the Khecarī and Bhūcarī [vidyās] shall be attained.
Everything arises from meditation alone; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Through the yoga of constant practice, one becomes perfected, and not otherwise.
This is the truth, the truth, and again the truth: he shall certainly become equal to me.
It is also found in the Yogaśāstra, delighting the yogins and bestowing upon them spiritual accomplishment. (5.150)
Now begins the exposition of the Royal Yoga (Rājayoga).
Hereafter, the thousand-petaled lotus of divine form stands outside the body known as the Egg of Brahmā, bestowing liberation. (5.151)
Kailāsa is the name of that very place where Maheśa resides;
he is called Nakula, the imperishable, free from decay and growth. (5.152)
By the mere knowledge of this state, for men there shall be no further birth in this saṃsāra;
and through the yoga of constant practice, they will possess the complete power to create and dissolve the entire aggregate of beings. (5.153)

With his mind settled here upon Kailāsa, the supreme abode of the swans, the yogi—whose heart-disease has been removed and whose vital breaths have been brought under control—lives for a long time, liberated from death. (5.154)
When the movement of the mind has dissolved into the Supreme Lord known as Kula, then, through the equilibrium of samādhi, the yogi attains immovability. (5.155)
When meditation is practiced without interruption, the forgetting of the world occurs;
then, the yogin certainly attains manifold powers. (5.156)
Therefore, the yogi should drink the nectar that has flowed down continuously;
having quickly brought death to death and conquered the *kula* within the lotus,
the power called *Kuṇḍalinī*, known as *Kulā*, attains dissolution there.
Then the fourfold creation dissolves into the Supreme Self.
Having known and attained that object by which the fluctuations of the mind dissolve, the yogi, free from all expectations, exerts himself toward it. (5.158)
When the fluctuations of the mind have dissolved into that [Self], the yogi certainly becomes established therein;
then he realizes himself as the stainless one, whose nature is undivided knowledge. (5.159)
Having visualized one's own symbolic form as described outside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
one should contemplate that great void after having entered into it, without contradiction.
Having practiced that which is empty of beginning, middle, and end, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns and resembling ten million moons, one shall attain perfection.
One should always practice this meditation day after day without laziness;
for him, complete perfection shall arise within a year—of this there is no doubt.
He whose mind becomes truly steady there for even half a moment [attains it].
That very yogi is a true devotee, honored in all the worlds.
The entire mass of his impurities perishes at that very moment. || 5.164 ||
Having seen that [reality], they no longer proceed upon the path of death and saṃsāra;
one should practice that with effort by means of the path of self-mastery (svādhiṣṭhāna). || 5-165 ||
The greatness of this meditation cannot be described by me;
he who accomplishes it and knows it is esteemed by us as well. (5.166)
Through meditation alone, one understands the arising of various visions;
endowed with the qualities such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest, one certainly becomes so—of this there is no doubt. (5.167)
The Rājayoga has been declared by me, which is hidden in all the tantras;
now I shall explain this Rājādhirājayoga in brief. (5.168)
Having assumed the svastika posture in a well-consecrated place free from living beings, and having diligently worshipped the Guru, one should practice this meditation. (5.169)
Having understood through the reasoning of Vedanta that the individual soul is without support, the wise man, having made his mind supportless, should not think of anything at all. (5.170)
From this meditation, great perfection certainly arises; there is no doubt.
Having made the mind free from fluctuations, one becomes the full form oneself. (5.171)
He who indeed constantly accomplishes this is a yogi free from longing;
there is no such thing as "I," for at all times only the Self exists. (5.172)
Who is bound, or whose is liberation? He who always perceives [all] as one—whosoever constantly acts thus is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (5.173)
That very yogi is a true devotee, honored in all worlds;

having realized "I am He," and having abandoned both the notions of "I" and "you" regarding the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), he should contemplate the indivisible whole.
The yogi, free from all attachments, should take refuge in that seed wherein everything is dissolved through superimposition and negation. (5.174)
Having abandoned the direct, full consciousness-bliss, those deluded by error—fools indeed—wander about, treating both the indirect and the direct as if they were one. (5.175)
That Supreme Brahman which makes this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings invisible, yet makes it visible—when abandoned, [the world] dissolves into that. (5.176)
Just as ignorance, which is the cause of [continued] existence, does not arise intensely, the yogi constantly practices that which is entirely free from attachment. (5.177)
Restraining all the senses from their objects, the wise man should remain free from attachment, as if in deep sleep, with regard to those very objects. (5.178)

For one who practices thus constantly, that which is self-luminous shines forth; the words of the guru cease to be necessary for the purpose of awakening the intellect capable of hearing, and by the power of that practice, a single, innate knowledge arises of its own accord. (5.179)
From which words turn back, along with the mind, having failed to reach it—
that stainless knowledge, arising from spiritual practice, certainly shines forth by itself.
Without Haṭha there is no Rājayoga, and without Rājayoga there is no Haṭha;
therefore, the yogi proceeds by means of Haṭha through the path of the true guru. (5.181)
While the body remains and he lives, he does not intensely practice yoga;
he lives for the enjoyment of the objects of the senses—of this there is no doubt. (5.182)
Until the culmination of the ripening of practice, there should be mindfulness of limited food;
for in this world, only a wise person who is without [worldly] support is able to perform the spiritual discipline.
In an assembly, the wise man should speak with exceedingly virtuous discourse;
for the sake of preserving his spiritual essence, he should avoid excessive talk.
"I renounce, I renounce, I utterly and completely renounce all attachment."
Otherwise, one shall not obtain liberation; this is the truth, the truth that I have spoken.
Practice is performed in secret, having abandoned attachment within that state;
however, for the sake of worldly interaction, one should act with an outward appearance of attachment.
All those born of action remain engaged in their respective duties.
In the act of making [an image], there is never any fault in using a mere sign (nimitta). || 5-185 ||
When one of sound intellect, even though being a householder, acts having thus resolved, then he attains perfection; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (5.186)
One who is liberated from both sin and merit, who has renounced the pursuit of bodily goals—
he would be liberated even while remaining at home as a householder;
a householder who is ever-yoked in yoga is not smeared by sins or merits.
Even while performing those sinful acts, he was engaged in his own duty for the sake of sustaining the world.
Oṃ aiḥ kliḥ striḥ!
Now I shall fully explain the supreme method for accomplishing the mantra, by which happiness in this world and the next may be attained without obstruction. (5.188)
When that supreme mantra is known, the perfection of yoga indeed occurs;
through that yoga, the sovereign lord of practitioners attains the bestowal of all sovereignty and happiness. (5.189)
In the *mūlādhāra* there is a lotus endowed with four petals;
in its center is the seed-syllable *vāgbhava*, flashing with the brilliance of lightning. (5.190)
In the heart is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), with the luster of the Bandhūka flower;
in the lotus of the Command (Ājñā-ravinda) is that called Śakti, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
These three seed-syllables are to be kept secret; they bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
A yogi who seeks to achieve perfection should practice these three mantras.
Having received this mantra from the guru, one should recite it with a mind free of doubt, neither too quickly nor too slowly, ensuring the proper junction of each syllable with the next. (5.192)
With his mind fixed on that and with single-minded concentration, the wise one, according to the procedure taught by the Teacher,
should offer a hundred thousand oblations before the Goddess and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.

At the conclusion of the recitation, the wise and intelligent practitioner should offer *karavīra* flowers combined with molasses, milk, and clarified butter into a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a womb (*yoni*). (5.194)
When the practice has been performed, the wise one will have completed the preliminary service;
thereafter, the goddess Tripurabhairavī indeed grants all desires.
Having pleased the Guru according to the rules and obtained the most excellent of mantras, even one of meager fortune attains success when joined with this procedure. (5.196)
If a practitioner who has conquered his senses recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times,
women afflicted by passion become agitated at the mere sight of him.
They fall before the practitioner, shameless and devoid of fear. || 5-197 ||
If one recites [the mantra] two hundred thousand times, those who reside in whatever realm they may be will come,
like to a sacred ford, having abandoned their family and physical form.
They give him their entire possessions and remain under his sole authority. || 5.198 ||

When recited three hundred thousand times in that manner, all those who belong to the maṇḍala, together with their maṇḍalas, come under one's control; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (5.199)
With six hundred thousand [arrows], he struck the protector of the earth along with his servants, troops, and vehicles.
When twelve hundred thousand recitations have been performed, all the lords of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and uragas come under one's control and constantly carry out one's commands.
For the wise and supreme practitioner who has recited [the mantra] three million five hundred thousand times,
even the perfected Vidyādharas and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases [will appear].
They all come under one's control; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Through forceful practice (*haṭha*), the knowledge of hearing and omniscience are produced. (5.202)
Likewise, by means of eighteen lakhs [of recitations],
the practitioner shall rise up, leaving this body behind, and become possessed of a divine body.
He wanders at will through the world, seeing the earth as full of vulnerabilities.
With twenty-eight hundred thousand [recitations], one becomes a lord of the Vidyādharas;
the wise practitioner shall become able to assume any form at will and possess great strength.
By reciting it thirty lakhs of times, one becomes equal to Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
by sixty lakhs, one attains the state of Rudra; and by eighty lakhs, immortality.
By means of ten million [repetitions], the great yogi merges into the supreme state;
such a yogi becomes a *sādhaka*, and he is exceedingly rare throughout the three worlds. (5.204)
In Tripura, there is but one Śiva, the supreme cause;
that state is imperishable, peaceful, immeasurable, and free from all ailment.
That wise person undoubtedly obtains everything he desires. || 5-205 ||
The Śiva-vidyā is the great vidyā, the Maheśvarī who is hidden even before [others]. Therefore, this scripture spoken by me should be concealed by the wise. (5.206)
The science of Haṭha must be kept strictly secret by a yogi desiring perfection;
it becomes potent when guarded, but powerless when revealed. (5.207)
The wise person who constantly recites this from beginning to end will,
without a doubt, attain the perfection of yoga in due course.
The wise one who worships this constantly attains liberation. || 5-208 ||
One should cause even all virtuous seekers of liberation to hear it;
for one who is engaged in the practice, success will come—how could it be otherwise for one who is inactive? (5.209)
Therefore, this should be performed by the best of yogis through the prescription of ritual action,
being content with whatever is obtained by chance and having completely abandoned internal conceptualization.
Even a householder who is unattached is liberated through the practice of yoga.
Success indeed comes to householders who are masters through the recitation [of mantras];
therefore, a householder should apply himself to the practice of yoga.
Having remained at home, filled with sons, wife, and so forth,
and having abandoned attachment within himself to the path of yoga,
he later becomes a householder upon perceiving the signs of spiritual accomplishment.
Having indeed accomplished the state of non-appropriation (mamatva), he should sport. || 5-212 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Yoga Śāstra, within the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, in the venerable Śiva Saṃhitā. May there be auspiciousness.
